answers.primary: Permission deny rules in the harness permission system, delivered through managed settings so no user or project file can loosen them: Read(./secrets/**) and Edit(./secrets/**) plus content-scoped Bash deny rules, combined with the Bash sandbox's sandbox.filesystem deny paths for OS-level coverage of subprocesses. The permissions docs state the point directly: use the permission system rather than a hook to enforce a hard allow or deny, and a managed-settings deny cannot be overridden by any other level including --allowedTools.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning a deny decision. Rejected because the hook layer is described as best-effort for this purpose (its Bash if filter fails open when the command cannot be parsed) and a hook decision never bypasses permission evaluation anyway, so the deny rule is doing the real work either way.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The check runs outside the model's judgment, evaluated deny-first on every tool call, which is exactly what turns a convention into a guarantee.
answers.context_boundary: Nothing crosses into the model as instruction text; the rule lives in settings and is applied by the harness before the tool executes, so the model only ever sees a blocked-tool result. A bare Bash deny even removes the tool from Claude's context. The same rule set is inherited by subagents and by agent-team teammates spawned from the session.
answers.lifecycle: Loaded at startup from the managed settings chain and evaluated on every tool call for the whole session, including resumed sessions. It stops applying only when the managed policy file itself is changed or removed, not by anything said in a prompt.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the tools the harness understands, but there is a documented gap: Read and Edit deny rules cover the built-in file tools and the Bash file commands Claude Code recognizes (cat, head, tail, sed), not an arbitrary python or node subprocess that opens the file itself, so without the sandbox the compliance claim is overstated. A second trap: writing Write(secrets/**) instead of Edit(secrets/**) is silently ineffective for file checks and only produces a startup warning.
answers.version_caveat: The managed-only keys (allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, allowManagedHooksOnly, strictPluginOnlyCustomization) are read from managed settings alone and have no effect in user or project files. A Read deny rule also blocking Edit on the same path requires v2.1.208 or later, so on earlier builds both rules must be written out. Sandboxing is a separate feature that must be enabled to get the OS-level half.

answers.primary: A project skill at .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md with the two helper scripts bundled beside it in scripts/ and referenced from the body through ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}, so the runbook body and the scripts are on disk rather than in context. This is precisely the progressive-disclosure property the team is asking for: skill descriptions load into context so Claude knows the skill exists, and the full content only loads when the skill is invoked.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md. Rejected because CLAUDE.md is injected as a user message on every session and stays resident for the whole conversation, which is the recurring token cost the team is complaining about.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness loads and renders the skill, but nothing forces Claude to execute all 400 lines in order once the content is in context.
answers.context_boundary: Main session context. Only the name plus description and when_to_use text sit in the skill listing between runs, truncated at 1,536 combined characters; the rendered body crosses in on invoke and then stays for the rest of the session. If even the once-a-week body is too heavy, context: fork runs the skill in its own subagent context and returns only the result.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered when someone types /release, or by Claude when the description matches. The rendered content persists in the conversation from that point on; Claude Code does not re-read the file on later turns, so standing instructions beat one-time steps. Auto-compaction re-attaches the most recent invocation, keeping the first 5,000 tokens per skill under a shared 25,000-token budget, so a long runbook can be truncated after a compaction.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory. A 400-line ordered procedure is exactly the shape that degrades: Claude can reorder, skip, or paraphrase steps, and the docs note that a skill can appear to stop influencing behavior while its text is still present. Put the irreversible parts in the helper scripts and gate them with permission rules rather than trusting the prose; re-invoke the skill after compaction to restore the body.
answers.version_caveat: No plan gate or flag. Re-invoking a skill whose rendered content is unchanged adds a short already-loaded note instead of a second full copy only from v2.1.202; earlier versions appended the whole body again on every re-invocation, which matters for a body this size. Nested .claude/skills resolution behavior changed in v2.1.203.

answers.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added over HTTP transport (claude mcp add --transport http tracker https://tracker.internal/mcp) at project scope so the config lives in a checked-in .mcp.json the whole team shares, with each developer completing the OAuth 2.0 flow individually from /mcp or claude mcp login. Claude then reads and updates tickets through the server's tools instead of anyone pasting ticket text.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that shells out to the tracker's REST API through Bash with a token in an environment variable. Rejected because it puts credential handling and pagination logic in prose the model has to follow, and it gives no OAuth token refresh, no tool schema, and no /mcp authentication surface.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the connection, the OAuth handshake, token storage and refresh, and which tools are exposed. The model owns whether and when to call those tools during a coding session.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context. Server tool definitions are loaded at startup and consume context proportional to how many tools the server exposes; tool call results (ticket bodies, comments) cross back into the conversation and stay there. MCP resources can also be pulled in explicitly with the @server:resource form.
answers.lifecycle: The server connects at session start and its tools stay available for the session; the token is refreshed automatically when a request returns 401 and the server is re-flagged in /mcp only if the retry also fails. It stops applying when the server is removed, disabled, or the scope it was added at is no longer in effect.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the individual call and open for the task: a 401 or 403 flags the server as needing authentication and the tool call errors, but Claude simply continues the coding work without the ticket data unless something else stops it. The other practical failure is context bloat from a chatty server, and mistaking a rejected headers.Authorization value for an OAuth problem (Claude Code reports a connection failure instead of falling back to OAuth in that case).
answers.version_caveat: OAuth works with HTTP transport, not WebSocket, which supports neither OAuth nor the --transport flag. claude mcp login <name> to run the flow outside a session requires v2.1.186 or later. The transient-refresh-failure fix (not flagging a server for the rest of the session after a network blip) landed in v2.1.206. A self-hosted server needing a pre-registered redirect URI needs --callback-port, and a nonstandard discovery chain needs authServerMetadataUrl.

answers.primary: A SessionStart hook configured in the repo's .claude/settings.json, running a command that queries the tracker and reads the current branch, and returning the result as hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (or simply on stdout, which SessionStart adds as context Claude can see). It runs before the first prompt, so every session in the repo opens already holding live data.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md. Rejected because it is static text committed to the repo: it cannot pull the sprint list or the branch at the moment the session opens, and it would go stale between edits.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns firing the hook and injecting its output. What Claude does with the injected sprint list and branch name afterwards is model-owned.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context, before the first user turn. Only the hook's stdout or additionalContext string crosses the boundary; the command runs as an ordinary subprocess outside any model context. Environment variables the hook writes to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE persist into later Bash commands in that session.
answers.lifecycle: Fires when a session begins or resumes, with the source matcher distinguishing startup, resume, clear, compact and fork; it re-runs on resume so the context is refreshed rather than replayed stale. It stops applying at session end, and it never fires mid-session, so a sprint change during a long session is not picked up.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. SessionStart hooks cannot block: a non-zero exit surfaces stderr to the user as a hook error notice and the session proceeds with no sprint context at all, silently degrading rather than stopping. The hook also runs on every session so a slow tracker query stalls startup, and because SessionStart typically fires before MCP servers finish connecting, an mcp_tool hook here should expect a not-connected error on first run.
answers.version_caveat: SessionStart supports only command and mcp_tool hook types; http, prompt and agent hooks are not available on this event. Exit-code-2 stderr renders in the transcript from v2.1.199, and only to the user, never to Claude. If the hook installs skills it must also return reloadSkills: true for them to be usable in the same session.

answers.primary: A plugin published through a private team marketplace, bundling the review helper as a skill (or agent), the lifecycle automations as hooks/hooks.json, and the tracker integration as .mcp.json at the plugin root, with an explicit version field in .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Consuming repos enable it through extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins, or the platform team force-enables it in managed settings so all 40 repos receive it without per-repo opt-in.
answers.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into each repository. Rejected because it gives no versioning and no update path: shipping a fix would mean 40 pull requests, which is exactly the distribution problem the plugin model solves.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns discovery, loading and version resolution of the plugin's components. Ownership of the behaviour inside splits per component: the bundled hooks are harness-enforced, the skill and MCP tools are model-invoked.
answers.context_boundary: Per consuming session. Plugin skill descriptions and plugin MCP tool definitions enter each session's context; hooks run out of context as subprocesses. Skills arrive namespaced as /plugin-name:skill-name, which is the deliberate cost of avoiding collisions across 40 repos.
answers.lifecycle: Loads when the plugin is enabled in a repo and stays active for every session there. Consumers receive an update only when the version field is bumped; /reload-plugins picks changes up without restarting. It stops applying on uninstall, on disable, or if managed settings force-disable it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at the distribution layer: a repo that never enables the plugin simply does not get the behaviour, and nothing reports the gap unless managed settings force-enable it. If version is omitted and the plugin is distributed by git, the commit SHA is used and every commit counts as a new version, so consumers churn. Component load errors are quiet too: they land in the /plugin Errors tab rather than failing the session.
answers.version_caveat: No plan gate for a self-hosted private marketplace, but submitting to the community marketplace via the claude.ai form requires a Team or Enterprise organization with directory management access (the Console form is the individual path). Passing a .zip to --plugin-dir requires v2.1.128 or later. Managed marketplace restrictions can block registering a marketplace, and --plugin-dir cannot override plugins that managed settings force-enable or force-disable.

answers.primary: A skill for the deploy procedure with disable-model-invocation: true in its frontmatter, so it can only be triggered by a human typing /deploy. This is the documented case for that field: you do not want Claude deciding to deploy because your code looks ready. Adding context: fork keeps the long procedure in its own subagent context.
answers.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md rule instructing Claude never to deploy unprompted. Rejected because it is advisory text competing with the model's own judgment, which is precisely the failure the requirement rules out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness for the trigger: the flag removes the skill from the model-invocable listing so Claude cannot load it on its own. The model still owns execution once a human has invoked it.
answers.context_boundary: The main session, or a forked subagent context if context: fork is set. The skill body crosses in only on explicit invocation and then persists for the rest of the session; with context: fork only the result returns to the main conversation.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when a person types /deploy (plus any $ARGUMENTS). It never self-triggers, and as of v2.1.196 it also will not run when a scheduled task fires with the skill as its prompt. The loaded content stops applying at session end.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the skill itself, but it is not a deploy lock. The flag prevents the skill from loading; it does nothing to stop Claude from running the same deploy commands directly through Bash if it decides to. To make the requirement real, pair it with an ask or deny permission rule on the deploy command, so the shell path is gated by the harness too.
answers.version_caveat: disable-model-invocation blocking a scheduled task whose prompt is the skill requires v2.1.196 or later; before that a scheduled trigger could still fire it. The related user-invocable: false field is the opposite restriction and must not be confused with it. No plan restriction applies.

answers.primary: A GitHub Action in the repository's workflow config, triggered on issues: opened, running Claude Code non-interactively against the issue payload to apply labels, search for duplicates and post the first-response comment. The scheduling comparison in the docs assigns exactly this class of work (tasks tied to repo events like opened PRs, living alongside your workflow config) to GitHub Actions rather than to anything that needs a local session.
answers.rejected_alternative: A routine running on Anthropic-managed infrastructure. It can trigger on GitHub events as well as a schedule, but it puts the trigger, the credentials and the audit trail outside the repository, whereas an Action keeps them versioned next to the code the triage depends on.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split. The harness (CI) owns the trigger and the fact that a run happens on every new issue; the model owns the triage quality, the label choice and the duplicate judgment, none of which are enforceable.
answers.context_boundary: A fresh headless session per workflow run, with no local user session and no carry-over between issues. The issue title, body and repo checkout cross in; labels and a comment cross out through the GitHub API or an MCP server. Nothing persists to the next run.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on the issues: opened webhook and ends when the job exits. It stops applying if the workflow file is removed, the event filter changes, or the credential secret expires.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: a failed or skipped job leaves the issue untriaged with nobody at a terminal to notice, so an explicit failure notification is required. The substantive risk is that the issue body is untrusted attacker-controlled text being fed to an agent that holds repo write, so the run should have narrowly scoped permissions and deny rules rather than broad tokens. Duplicate detection also produces false positives that no human reviews.
answers.version_caveat: I cannot state the action's own version requirements, required token scopes or workflow permissions from my permitted inputs: the documentation mirror I have contains only the row in the scheduling comparison pointing at the GitHub Actions page, and that page is not included. Treat the action version, its authentication method and any plan requirement as unverified here.

answers.primary: An agent team: a lead session that spawns five teammates, each assigned one hypothesis, instructed to message each other and try to disprove the others' theories, converging on a findings document. This is the documented use case almost verbatim (debugging with competing hypotheses, teammates talking to each other like a scientific debate), and teammates messaging each other directly is the capability that makes the adversarial structure possible.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents. Rejected because subagents only report results back to the main agent and never talk to each other, so there is no back-and-forth and no cross-examination, only five parallel reports that the lead would have to reconcile alone.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides task assignment, when the debate has converged and what the consensus is; the harness only supplies the mailbox, the shared task list with file-locked claiming, and the panel.
answers.context_boundary: Five independent context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads project context (CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, skills) the same way a regular session does but does not inherit the lead's conversation history, so hypothesis details must be written into the spawn prompt. What crosses between them is SendMessage traffic, task-list state, and the shared findings file on disk.
answers.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate is spawned and lives for the lead session. Teammates go idle and notify the lead when done; a shutdown request per teammate ends one gracefully. The team config directory is removed at session exit, while the task list persists locally for resumed sessions.
answers.failure_mode: Token cost scales linearly with five separate Claude instances, and coordination is where it breaks: task status lags when a teammate forgets to mark completion, blocking dependents; the lead may start investigating itself instead of waiting, or declare consensus early; teammates are not isolated in worktrees, so if the debate turns into edits they overwrite each other. Advisory throughout: nothing forces a teammate to actually attack the others' theories.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment; without it no team is set up and Claude will not spawn teammates. The setup flow described here is v2.1.178 and later (TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist, cleanup is automatic). Split-pane display needs tmux or iTerm2 with it2 and is unavailable in VS Code's integrated terminal, Windows Terminal and Ghostty; in-process teammates are not restored by /resume.

answers.primary: A custom output style saved at the project level in .claude/output-styles/, defining the data-analyst role and the fixed tabular report format, with keep-coding-instructions left at its default of false so Claude Code's built-in software engineering instructions are dropped rather than merely supplemented. Output styles are the mechanism that modifies the system prompt itself and applies to every response, which is what a per-turn format requirement needs.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md. Rejected because it adds a user message after the system prompt and cannot remove the default engineering instructions; the requirement here is explicitly to take those out, not to layer project conventions on top of them.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The style is system-prompt text plus periodic adherence reminders; nothing in the harness validates that a reply actually came back as a table.
answers.context_boundary: The main conversation only. The style text is appended to the system prompt at session start. Subagents run their own system prompt and are unaffected, so any delegated work comes back in default voice; a fork is the exception because it inherits the parent's full system prompt.
answers.lifecycle: Read once at session start, so a change takes effect only after /clear or a new session. It then applies to every turn until the outputStyle setting is changed. Selecting it from /config writes to .claude/settings.local.json, which is per-developer, so committing outputStyle to the project settings file is what makes it apply to everyone on the project.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory, and it drifts: long sessions wander off the fixed format, which is why the adherence reminders exist, and heavy tool output can pull replies back toward prose. Removing the coding instructions is a real trade: if anyone in this project does need file edits, the scoping, verification and comment conventions are gone. Output tokens also rise or fall entirely according to what the style tells Claude to produce.
answers.version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; use /config or set outputStyle directly. Nested project output-styles directories resolve nearest-to-working-directory as of v2.1.178. If the style is shipped inside a plugin, force-for-plugin applies it automatically and overrides the user's outputStyle setting.

answers.primary: A headless Claude Code invocation pinned in the CI job (claude -p with the prompt file checked into the repo), launched with the discovery surfaces explicitly cut off: --bare to skip auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, or, if some project config is wanted, --setting-sources naming exactly the sources allowed plus --strict-mcp-config so only servers from an in-repo --mcp-config are used. The Agent SDK is the same shape if the job needs to post-process results programmatically.
answers.rejected_alternative: A project skill holding the typo and lint instructions. Rejected because it makes the instruction set another discovered configuration source, and it does nothing about the teammate's user-level hooks or the machine's MCP config, which is the actual leak being guarded against.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness for what loads: the flags deterministically decide which config sources are read, and that part is not up to the model. The content of the review is model-owned.
answers.context_boundary: One non-interactive session per CI run, with nothing carried between runs. The diff crosses in on stdin or as the prompt argument, findings cross out on stdout (use --output-format json so the job can parse them). No user session, no local state.
answers.lifecycle: Runs once per pull request when the CI job executes and ends when the process exits. It stops applying when the job is removed from the pipeline; there is no resident configuration to go stale.
answers.failure_mode: The configuration half fails closed, the reproducibility half does not: identical flags make the loaded config identical, but the model's output is not byte-for-byte deterministic, and the model version the job resolves to can change under it. So the promise you can actually keep is a reproducible environment, not a reproducible string. Also be aware --bare narrows Claude to Bash, file read and file edit tools, so a prompt that assumed an MCP tool silently loses it.
answers.version_caveat: --bare sets CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE and is the fastest way to strip discovery; do not substitute --safe-mode (v2.1.169 and later), which disables customizations but still applies managed settings policy including policy-configured hooks, so it is not equivalent for isolation. Whether managed policy also survives --bare is not spelled out in the documentation I have, so pin the runner image if that matters. --strict-mcp-config does not filter servers passed inline via --agents or the SDK agents option, since those count as explicit caller input.
